sections.name: Hook
sections.markdown:
Press the tip of your tongue to the little ridge just behind your upper teeth — that bump is
where English keeps its t and d. Now slide the tip back, past the ridge, and curl it up
toward the dome of your mouth. Tap. That half-centimeter journey is the whole lesson. The
place has the tradition's most vivid name — मूर्धन्य, "of the crown of the head" — and the
sounds made there are the ones the world associates with India, though your English t lives
right next door and Swedish quietly makes them too. Row three of five: ट ठ ड ढ ण — the same
five manner slots you have now run twice, one new tongue-curl, and twelve new words, one of
them the favorite object of Indian philosophy: a clay pot.

sections.name: Previous Lesson Review
sections.markdown:
पिछले पाठों की पुनरावृत्ति — answer from memory *before* looking anything up.

1. **The row first:** name the five manner slots of every varga, in order — the frame you
   have now used for two rows.
2. **Recite both rows aloud:** क ख ग घ ङ (ka kha ga gha ṅa), then च छ ज झ ञ
   (ca cha ja jha ña) — with the tissue check on the aspirates.
3. Which letter of the velar row throws the tissue hardest — and which barely stirs it?
4. **Dictation from memory:** write जल चलति — the water word and the course's first verb,
   both from the palatal lesson. Say it aloud as you write: every vowel full.
5. **Chapter 2 interval item:** in अंक (aṃka), which nasal does the dot stand for — and why
   that one?

<details><summary>उत्तराणि · Answers</summary>

1. Voiceless, voiceless aspirated, voiced, voiced breathy, nasal.
2. क ख ग घ ङ · च छ ज झ ञ — the aspirates ख and छ flutter the tissue.
3. ख throws it; क barely moves it — that stillness is the un-aspirating work of the row.
4. जल (jala) "water"; चलति (calati) "moves". Four full vowels between them — no "jal", no
   "calti".
5. [ŋ] — the nasal of क's own varga: before a stop, anusvāra is pronounced at that stop's
   place (v1.c02.l06). Hold the thought: today the retroflex family gets its own nasal, ण.
</details>

sections.name: Historical Context
sections.markdown:
ऐतिहासिक सन्दर्भः — a row named for the crown of the head, and a sound family with
passports.

In the sound map (v1.c01.l02) you toured the mouth's five stations from throat to lips.
Today's station wears the tradition's boldest label:

> **[TRADITION · परम्परा]** The traditional phonetics texts — the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā and the
> Prātiśākhyas — file ट ठ ड ढ ण as मूर्धन्य (mūrdhanya), from मूर्धन् (mūrdhan) "head,
> crown": sounds made with the tongue reaching up toward the dome that crowns the mouth's
> interior. The name is an articulation diagram compressed into one word.

> **[HISTORY · इतिहासः]** Retroflexion is one of South Asia's great shared features:
> Sanskrit and its Indo-Aryan descendants have it, and the neighboring Dravidian family
> (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) uses it even more richly — a convergence built over
> millennia of contact. But the sound type holds no passport: Swedish and Norwegian produce
> retroflex [ʈ ɖ ɳ] in their *rt, rd, rn* words, and several Australian languages maintain
> full retroflex series of their own. [REF:masica1991]

So if you have heard that these sounds are "unique to Indian languages" — a claim the old
edition of this course repeated — file it under charming but false. India is where
retroflexion is *richest* and most systematic, not where it is alone. And English? English
is the near-miss case: its t and d stop at the ridge, one small curl short of the crown.
That nearness is today's best tool and, as §12 will show, today's best trap.

sections.name: Scientific Explanation
sections.markdown:
वैज्ञानिक व्याख्या — what a retroflex is, and why your English t is both friend and foe.

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** ट ठ ड ढ ण are retroflex stops — /ʈ ʈʰ ɖ ɖʱ ɳ/: the tongue **tip**
> curls up and back to strike the roof of the mouth *behind* the alveolar ridge. The curled
> posture opens a small hollow beneath the tongue, which is why retroflexes ring darker and
> more cavernous than their front-of-the-mouth cousins. [REF:ladefoged2015]

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** English t and d are alveolar — made *at* the ridge. On the mouth's
> map that puts them closer to retroflex ट/ड than to dental त/द: one small retraction away
> from the first, a full tongue-posture change away from the second. English ears therefore
> accept an alveolar t as "close enough" for either row — which is exactly why the dental
> row (next lesson) will need an explicit teeth-contact contrast. [REF:ladefoged2015]

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** The manner frame is unchanged: voiceless, voiceless aspirated,
> voiced, voiced breathy, nasal. Only the *place* is new — master one tongue-curl and all
> five letters follow. [REF:whitney1889 §§39–50]

Three consequences. **First, this lesson is a movement, not a mystery.** You are not
learning five alien sounds; you are learning one gesture — curl and tap — and running the
row you already own through it. **Second, train your ear on the ring.** A retroflex tap
sounds darker and hollower than an alveolar one; record yourself alternating English "ta"
and ट and listen for the change of room-tone. **Third, respect the near-miss.** Because
English t/d sit next door, your tongue will happily settle at the ridge and call it done.
The fix is physical, not acoustic: feel whether the tip actually traveled past the bump
(§11). Close enough to fool the ear is not close enough to be the sound.

sections.name: Sanskrit Explanation
sections.markdown:
संस्कृतव्याख्या — the lesson's idea in the simplest possible Sanskrit.

ट इति मूर्धन्यः वर्णः।
(ṭa iti mūrdhanyaḥ varṇaḥ.) "*ṭa* is a retroflex sound." — ट मूर्धन्य वर्ण है।

ट ठ ड ढ ण — एते मूर्धन्याः।
(ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa — ete mūrdhanyāḥ.) "ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa — these are retroflexes." —
ट ठ ड ढ ण — ये सब मूर्धन्य हैं।

घटः अत्र अस्ति।
(ghaṭaḥ atra asti.) "The pot is here." — घड़ा यहाँ है।

Savor the last line: it is fully readable, letter by letter — घ from the velar lesson, ट
from today, and the tail ः is the visarga you have owned since v1.c02.l06. इति is doing its
usual quoting work, and the sentence-name for today's family, टवर्गः (ṭavargaḥ), is built
from ट itself plus वर्ग "group, row". Returning terms: वर्ण (varṇa) "speech sound", मूर्धन्य
(mūrdhanya) "retroflex", and the word वर्ग from the velar lesson. As throughout Volume 1,
each word is read whole, in careful pause form — connected speech knits words together by
sandhi rules that arrive in Volume 3.

sections.name: Hindi Explanation
sections.markdown:
हिन्दी व्याख्या

आज की पंक्ति पर आपका जन्मसिद्ध अधिकार है। टमाटर से ढोल तक, ठीक से डाल तक — मूर्धन्य
ध्वनियाँ आपकी जीभ दिन-भर बनाती रहती है। अंग्रेज़ी-भाषी साथी आज जीभ मोड़ना *सीख* रहे हैं;
आपको बस उस काम पर ध्यान देना सीखना है जो आप पहले से करते आए हैं। फिर भी — और अब तक आप इस
"फिर भी" के अभ्यस्त हो चुके हैं — हिन्दी की तीन आदतें यहाँ संस्कृत से टकराती हैं।

पहली आदत — बिन्दीवाले ड़ और ढ़। ये दोनों अक्षर हिन्दी की अपनी कमाई हैं: सदियों के बोलचाल
में स्वरों के बीच का ड घिसकर एक हल्का झटका बन गया, और लिखाई ने उसे नीचे बिन्दी देकर ड़ लिख
दिया — सड़क, पढ़ना, गुड़। यह झटका आपकी ज़बान की स्वचालित आदत है। पर संस्कृत की वर्णमाला में
ड़ है ही नहीं। इसलिए संस्कृत का गुड पढ़ते समय आदत को उल्टा घुमाइए: जीभ पूरा स्पर्श करे,
पूरा ठहरे — गु-ड, झटका नहीं, ठोस ठहराव। मज़ेदार बात यह कि हिन्दी का गुड़ इसी संस्कृत गुड का
घिसा-चला वंशज है — एक ही शब्द, दो भाषाएँ, और बीच में बस वही झटके वाला सफ़र।

दूसरी आदत — ण को न कह देना। लिखते समय हम गुण, बाण, कारण में ण ठीक-ठीक लिखते हैं, पर बोलचाल
में प्रायः "गुन", "बान", "कारन" ही निकलता है। संस्कृत में यह छूट नहीं है: ण अपनी पूरी
मूर्धन्य गूँज के साथ बोला जाता है — जीभ की नोक मुड़ी रहे, और गूँज नाक से उठे। गुण कहते समय
अपनी जीभ से पूछिए: नोक सचमुच मुड़ी है, या दाँतों के पास आराम कर रही है?

तीसरी आदत पुरानी परिचित है — अन्तिम अ। घट है gha-ṭa: दो अक्षर, दोनों पूरे। ज़बान "घट्"
कहना चाहेगी; श्रुतलेख उसे मिनटों में पकड़ लेगा। तट, गण, कण — हर शब्द का अन्तिम अ अपनी पूरी
हाज़िरी माँगता है।

और अन्त में आज का उपहार, जो अब इस पाठमाला की परम्परा बन चला है: हिन्दी का घड़ा संस्कृत के
इसी घट की पीढ़ियों में ढली हुई सन्तान है — वही मिट्टी का बर्तन, वही शब्द, बीच में बस वही
ड-से-ड़ वाला रास्ता। आज आप घड़े के पुरखे से मिल रहे हैं।

sections.name: English Explanation
sections.markdown:
One new gesture — curl the tip back and tap the dome — and the manner row you have now run
twice does the rest. Third varga, fastest lesson so far. Letter cards: 🖼
`planned:assets/images/volume-1/v1c03l03-tta-varga-cards.svg`.

### The five cards — equal members, honest workloads

**ट** (ṭa) · /ʈ/ — the plain one. Curl, tap, release — and *no* puff of breath. The s-trick
from the velar lesson transfers: the t of English *stop* is unaspirated; now say it with
the tip curled back. Common everywhere: घट, तट, कटु.

**ठ** (ṭha) · /ʈʰ/ — the tissue-thrower of this row. Same curl, released with a hard puff.
You have been saying it since day one, in पाठः 🔊 "lesson". Rarely opens a native Sanskrit
word; frequent inside — the honest note on its card.

**ड** (ḍa) · /ɖ/ — the voiced one. Fingertips on your throat: the buzz must be running
*before* the release. Word-initially uncommon, word-internally at home: गुड.

**ढ** (ḍha) · /ɖʱ/ — the breathy-voiced one. The घ-skill from the velar row, relocated:
voice humming *through* a breathy release, tissue moving *and* throat buzzing. Few native
words start with it; it earns its keep inside words: गूढ, मूढ.

**ण** (ṇa) · /ɳ/ — the row's nasal. Curl the tip, hold it curled, and hum through the
nose. Essentially no Sanskrit word begins with ण — say so plainly — yet it is anything but
rare: गुण, गण, कण, तृण. Volume 4 tells the famous story of *why* so many words contain ण —
a rule (called ṇatva) that turns n into ṇ under retroflex influence. One line now, full
treatment there.

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** Frequency, honestly: ट is common in all positions; ठ ड ढ begin few
> native Sanskrit words but occur freely word-internally; ण essentially never opens a word
> and is everywhere inside them. Equal cards, unequal workloads — both facts on the same
> card. [REF:apte1890]

### The payoff — reading, worked out

- **घट** = घ + ट → gha-ṭa "pot" — breathy velar, then plain retroflex: a two-letter manner
  workout
- **गुण** = गु + ण → gu-ṇa "quality" — the curled nasal in its natural habitat
- **तृण** = तृ + ण → tṛ-ṇa "grass" — the below-sign ृ (v1.c02.l03) meets today's ण
- **गूढ** = गू + ढ → gū-ḍha "hidden" — long ऊ, then the breathy ढ held to the end

Twelve words today (§14), every one readable, every one using at least one letter that did
not exist for you yesterday.

sections.name: Pronunciation
sections.markdown:
उच्चारणम् — four drills, in order. Audio: 🔊
`planned:assets/audio/volume-1/v1c03l03-varga-drill.mp3` (drills 1–3) and
`planned:assets/audio/volume-1/v1c03l03-word-list.mp3` (drill 4 words).

**Drill 1 — the ridge walk (find the curl).** Rest the tongue tip behind your upper teeth.
Slide it slowly backward: the first bump is the alveolar ridge — English t's home. Keep
going, past the bump, curling the tip up until it points at the dome of the mouth. Tap once:
that contact is ट-position. Walk the path five times — teeth, ridge, dome — until the
three stations feel like three floors of one building.

**Drill 2 — the varga recital, third run.** ट ठ ड ढ ण (ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa), with the full
check kit: tissue still on ठ's puff, fingertips on the throat for ड's buzz, both at once
for ढ, nose-hum with the tip *held curled* for ण. Three slow rounds, one brisk. Then chain
the tour so far: क ख ग घ ङ · च छ ज झ ञ · ट ठ ड ढ ण — three rows, one breath each.

**Drill 3 — the syllable grid.** Read across, then down; long vowels get their two beats:

| टि /ʈi/ | टु /ʈu/ | टा /ʈɑː/ |
|---|---|---|
| ठि /ʈʰi/ | ठु /ʈʰu/ | ठो /ʈʰoː/ |
| डि /ɖi/ | डे /ɖeː/ | डा /ɖɑː/ |
| ढु /ɖʱu/ | ढो /ɖʱoː/ | ढी /ɖʱiː/ |
| णि /ɳi/ | णा /ɳɑː/ | णू /ɳuː/ |

**Drill 4 — one English word, three tongues.** Say English "tap" three ways: (1) as habit —
tip at the ridge; (2) tip curled back — you just said something close to ट; (3) tip pressed
on the teeth — a preview of next lesson's त. Same manner, three floors. Feeling the
*commute* between them is the skill; the dental floor gets its own lesson next. Finish with
§14 words from the audio: precision first, speed never.

sections.name: IPA
sections.markdown:
The new row: **/ʈ ʈʰ ɖ ɖʱ ɳ/**. Look at the symbols — ʈ, ɖ and ɳ each hang a rightward
hook off their base. That hook is the IPA's mark for retroflexion: the alphabet literally
draws the curled-back tip into the letters. The manner marks carry over from the velar row
unchanged: ʰ = voiceless puff, ʱ = breathy murmur.

**Narrow notes.** English t/d are plain alveolar [t] [d] — no hook. Next lesson's dentals
will wear a bridge underneath instead: [t̪]. One symbol-row tells the whole three-place
story: t̪ (teeth) — t (ridge) — ʈ (curled past the ridge). And one small word makes a fine
IPA field trip: तृण /t̪r̩ɳɐ/ — dental t̪, syllabic r̩ (v1.c02.l03), retroflex ɳ, and the
full final /ɐ/ — four course landmarks in four symbols.

Phonemic slashes, as always, mark meaning-bearing categories: /ʈ/ and /t̪/ are different
phonemes in Sanskrit, and the dental lesson will drill the pairs that prove it. Today's job
is to give /ʈ/ a home of its own, clearly past the ridge, so tomorrow's contrast has two
distinct addresses to work with.

sections.name: Mouth Position
sections.markdown:
मुखस्थानम् — walkthrough of the diagram (planned:
`assets/diagrams/volume-1/v1c03l03-retroflex-tongue.svg` — sagittal view with the tip
curled to the post-alveolar dome, the sub-lingual hollow shaded, and a three-position inset:
teeth · ridge · curl).

To find ट /ʈ/ and its row:

1. **Jaw:** relaxed, slightly open — the tip needs room to travel.
2. **Tip:** up and back. Touch the ridge first (the English station), then slide past it
   until the tip — or slightly its underside — meets the dome. The exact depth varies from
   speaker to speaker; the non-negotiable is *past the bump*.
3. **Seal and release:** close firmly, let pressure build for an instant, release crisply.
   For ड ढ, start the throat-buzz before the release; for ण, hold the curl while the sound
   flows through the nose.
4. **Listen for the room-tone:** the curled posture opens a hollow under the tongue, and
   the release rings darker — deeper "room sound" than an English t.

**Feel checks — this is a feel lesson, not a mirror lesson.** The action hides behind the
teeth, so the mirror that served उ/ऊ retires today; your instrument is the tip itself.
Check one: after saying ट, freeze — is the ridge-bump *in front of* your contact point? It
must be. Check two: alternate English "ta" and ट ten times and feel the tip commute; if
nothing moves, nothing changed. Check three: record the alternation and listen for the
darker ring on every second syllable.

sections.name: Common Mistakes
sections.markdown:
सामान्य-भ्रान्तयः — real errors, each with its fix. These feed the quiz distractors.

1. **Settling at the ridge (English speakers).** English t/d live one door away, so the
   tongue stops at its usual station and the ear shrugs: close enough. It is not the sound —
   the ring is too bright, the curl absent. *Fix:* trust feel over ear (§11): the tip must
   travel *past* the bump. Exaggerate the curl at first — aim deeper than you think you
   need — then relax toward normal as the audio comparisons start matching.
2. **The ड़-flap between vowels (Hindi speakers).** Hindi automatically turns intervocalic
   ड into the flap ड़ — so गुड comes out as गुड़, a grazing tap instead of a full stop.
   Sanskrit has no ड़. *Fix:* full contact, full stop: let the tongue *park* for an instant
   — गु-ड — before releasing. If you can feel a moment of complete silence at the closure,
   the stop is real; a flap has no such silence.
3. **ढ under-breathed.** Learners who mastered ट vs ठ still let ढ collapse into ड — voice
   without the murmur. *Fix:* the tissue-plus-throat double check: on ढ the tissue must
   move *and* the buzz must run through the breathy release, exactly as you trained on घ in
   the velar lesson. Drill the pair ड — ढ · ड — ढ until the tissue reports a difference.
4. **ण read as plain न-type [n] (Hindi speakers above all — and everyone else too).**
   Colloquial Hindi says "गुन" for गुण, and English has only the one n. In Sanskrit the
   retroflex nasal is its own phoneme. *Fix:* curl first, hum second — the tip must already
   be curled when the nasal starts, and stay curled through it. Ask mid-hum: where is my
   tip? If it is resting near the teeth, the sound is not ण.

sections.name: Examples
sections.markdown:
उदाहरणानि — a pot with a philosophical career, a synonym pair, one word with range, and a
breathy rhyme.

### घट — the philosophers' pot

**घट** (ghaṭa) "pot" — घड़ा · /gʱɐʈɐ/ [REF:apte1890 s.v. घट]

A humble clay water-pot — and the most argued-about object in Sanskrit intellectual
history.

> **[TRADITION · परम्परा]** In the Nyāya school of Indian logic, the pot is the stock
> example-object: घटः अस्ति (ghaṭaḥ asti) "the pot exists" is the demonstration sentence a
> beginning logic student meets on page one, the way English philosophy reaches for
> Socrates. Where an argument needs "some thing", the tradition hands it a pot.

### तट and कूल — two words, one riverbank

**तट** (taṭa) "shore, bank" — तट, किनारा · /t̪ɐʈɐ/

You already own कूल (kūla) "bank" from v1.c02.l02 — today its synonym arrives, and your
first synonym pair is complete: two words, one riverbank. Sanskrit's wealth of synonyms is
a feature you will meet again and again. As a bonus, तट is a one-word articulation drill:
the tongue starts at the teeth for त and curls back for ट — two stops, two floors, four
letters.

### गुण — a word with range

**गुण** (guṇa) "quality, strand" — गुण · /guɳɐ/

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** गुण's dictionary entry fans out from the concrete to the abstract: a
> strand or cord — of a rope, a bowstring — then a quality, an attribute, a virtue.
> One concrete image carrying a family of abstract senses is a pattern Sanskrit vocabulary
> loves; you will watch this particular word work hard across the whole tradition.
> [REF:apte1890 s.v. गुण]

### गूढ and मूढ — the breathy rhymes

**गूढ** (gūḍha) "hidden, secret" — गूढ़, छिपा · /guːɖʱɐ/
**मूढ** (mūḍha) "deluded, fool" — मूढ़, मूर्ख · /muːɖʱɐ/

A rhyme pair with a built-in joke — the hidden thing (गूढ) and the one it stays hidden
from (मूढ) — and two chances per breath at the row's hardest letter: long vowel, then ढ
with the murmur held all the way through.

sections.name: Vocabulary
sections.markdown:
शब्दावली — twelve words, all readable, no 🔊 crutches. Audio: 🔊
`planned:assets/audio/volume-1/v1c03l03-word-list.mp3` (model reading, each word twice).

| देवनागरी | IAST | IPA | English | हिन्दी | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| घट | ghaṭa | /gʱɐʈɐ/ | pot | घड़ा | the philosophers' object (§13); breathy घ + plain ट |
| तट | taṭa | /t̪ɐʈɐ/ | shore, bank | तट, किनारा | synonym of कूल (v1.c02.l02); teeth-to-curl drill |
| कटु | kaṭu | /kɐʈu/ | pungent, bitter | कड़वा, तीखा | a taste word; short उ, fully pronounced |
| जटा | jaṭā | /d͡ʑɐʈɑː/ | matted hair | जटा | the ascetic's locks; two beats on टा |
| कूट | kūṭa | /kuːʈɐ/ | peak; trick | चोटी; छल | one word, two lives — mountain-top and deception |
| गुण | guṇa | /guɳɐ/ | quality, strand | गुण | the range word (§13); tip curled for ण |
| गण | gaṇa | /gɐɳɐ/ | group, troop | गण, समूह | गुण/गण — one mātrā apart, keep them distinct |
| कण | kaṇa | /kɐɳɐ/ | particle, grain | कण | rhymes with गण; final अ full |
| तृण | tṛṇa | /t̪r̩ɳɐ/ | grass, blade | तिनका, घास | ृ below (v1.c02.l03) + ण; IPA field trip (§10) |
| गुड | guḍa | /guɖɐ/ | jaggery, raw sugar | गुड़ | Sanskrit keeps the full stop — no flap (§7, §12) |
| गूढ | gūḍha | /guːɖʱɐ/ | hidden, secret | गूढ़, छिपा | breathy ढ held to the end; rhymes with मूढ |
| मूढ | mūḍha | /muːɖʱɐ/ | deluded, fool | मूढ़, मूर्ख | the rhyme's other half (§13) |

Reading protocol, as always: block by block first (गु-ण), then the whole word at natural
speed, then check against the audio. Every retroflex gets a genuine curl, every dīrgha its
two beats, every final vowel its full /ɐ/ — घट is *ghaṭa*, never "ghaṭ".

sections.name: Grammar
sections.markdown:
व्याकरणम् — in Volume 1 this is a **script section**: five new letters, their strokes, and
two look-alike alarms.

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** Four of today's letters — ट ठ ड ढ — carry no right-hand vertical
> stem; ण is the row's only stem-bearer. Mātrās adapt without new rules: ि and ी stand in
> their usual places (टि, टी), and the below-signs hang from the base of the curve — टु,
> टू, as they hang from ट's bowl. Position is graphics; order is speech — unchanged.
> [REF:masica1991 ch.6]

### Stroke order — ट ठ ड ढ ण

One common convention, described here; teaching traditions vary in details. (Card:
`planned:assets/images/volume-1/v1c03l03-stroke-order.svg`; tracing:
`planned:assets/worksheets/volume-1/v1c03l03-tracing.pdf`.)

- **ट** — one continuous stroke: start at the top left, travel right, then dive down and
  sweep around to the left into an **open bowl**; headline last, riding on top.
- **ठ** — the same journey, but the curve keeps going and **closes into a full loop**,
  joining back where it began; headline last. The shape logic pair: ट open, ठ closed —
  when in doubt, ask "did the curve come home?"
- **ड** — a ट-like top and bowl, but the tail turns **inward** at the base, curling back
  into the bowl before it stops; headline last.
- **ढ** — write the ड path, then let the tail run on into one more loop before ending —
  the breathy letter carries extra ink, the same "more sound, more material" logic as आ and
  ऊ before it.
- **ण** — three strokes: a small loop at the left flowing into a wave that rises rightward;
  the vertical stem on the right; headline last. The row's only letter that hangs laundry
  on a stem.

**Look-alike alarm 1 — ट vs ठ:** open bowl vs closed loop, nothing else differs. **Alarm 2
— ड vs ङ:** the velar nasal ङ (v1.c03.l01) ends in a detached **dot**; ड ends in an
attached inward **curl**. Dot = velar hum; curl = voiced retroflex. Write the two side by
side once now, label them, and the confusion dies early.

### The grid gains its third row

| Manner slot | Letter | IAST | IPA | Check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| voiceless | ट | ṭa | /ʈ/ | tissue barely moves |
| voiceless aspirated | ठ | ṭha | /ʈʰ/ | tissue jumps |
| voiced | ड | ḍa | /ɖ/ | throat buzzes before release |
| voiced breathy | ढ | ḍha | /ɖʱ/ | buzz and warm breath together |
| nasal | ण | ṇa | /ɳ/ | nose hums, tip stays curled |

Three rows down, two to go — and the next one lives on your teeth.

sections.name: Conversation
sections.markdown:
सम्भाषणम् — two turns beside a water-pot. 🔊 audio recorded into the Chapter 3 drill pack
(§27).

— घटः अत्र अस्ति?
(ghaṭaḥ atra asti?) "Is the pot here?" — घड़ा यहाँ है?

— आम्, घटः अत्र अस्ति। जलम् अत्र अस्ति।
(ām, ghaṭaḥ atra asti. jalam atra asti.) "Yes, the pot is here. The water is here." —
हाँ, घड़ा यहाँ है। जल यहाँ है।

Notice what has quietly happened: घटः is readable to the last mark — stem word from today,
visarga tail from v1.c02.l06. जलम् is the palatal lesson's जल wearing the -म् tail you met
on कूलम् in Chapter 2: a noun ending (Volume 3) whose final म् needs the virāma sign
(Chapter 5). Read जल and let the audio close the word. Glue words, old friends: आम् (ām)
"yes" 🔊, अत्र (atra) "here" 🔊, अस्ति (asti) "is" 🔊. Every word in careful pause form —
the Volume 1 convention (§6).

sections.name: Story
sections.markdown:
कथा — घटः तटे? No — simpler and honest: **the pot on the riverbank**, in five pause-form
lines. Words readable in full are **bold**; glue words and grammar tails are glossed below.
Each line: Devanagari, IAST, English, Hindi.

1. **कमला** — **माता**! पश्य! **तटः**!
   (kamalā — mātā! paśya! taṭaḥ!) "Kamalā: Mother! Look — the riverbank!" —
   कमला — माँ! देखो! किनारा!
2. **माता** — आम्। जलम् अत्र अस्ति।
   (mātā — ām. jalam atra asti.) "Mother: Yes. The water is here." — माँ — हाँ। जल यहाँ है।
3. **कमला** — पश्य! **घटः**! **घटः** अत्र अस्ति!
   (kamalā — paśya! ghaṭaḥ! ghaṭaḥ atra asti!) "Kamalā: Look! A pot! There is a pot here!"
   — कमला — देखो! घड़ा! घड़ा यहाँ है!
4. **माता** — **घटः**? **कुतः** **घटः**?
   (mātā — ghaṭaḥ? kutaḥ ghaṭaḥ?) "Mother: A pot? From where, a pot?" —
   माँ — घड़ा? घड़ा कहाँ से?
5. **कमला** — **मम** **घटः**! **मम** **तटः**! **मम** जलम्!
   (kamalā — mama ghaṭaḥ! mama taṭaḥ! mama jalam!) "Kamalā: My pot! My riverbank! My
   water!" — कमला — मेरा घड़ा! मेरा किनारा! मेरा जल!

Yes — the same Kamalā who claimed मम कूलम् on this very riverbank in Chapter 2 has upgraded
her vocabulary: last time the bank was कूल, today it is its synonym तट, and this time she
can read every letter of her claim, visarga included. Glue words 🔊: पश्य (paśya) "look!",
आम् (ām) "yes", अत्र (atra) "here", अस्ति (asti) "is"; कुतः (kutaḥ) "from where?" returns
from the Chapter 2 story — and is now fully readable. Only जलम् still wears an unreadable
tail (§16).

> **[TRADITION · परम्परा]** One more thing today's letters can spell: कठ (kaṭha) — the name
> of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, the celebrated dialogue in which young Naciketas questions Death
> itself. Its story waits for Volume 5; as of today, you can read its name.

sections.name: Exercises
sections.markdown:
अभ्यासाः — six exercises; 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 are production tasks. Do them in order.

**अभ्यासः 1 · लेखनम् (tracing & writing).** Print or open the tracing worksheet ✍
(`planned:assets/worksheets/volume-1/v1c03l03-tracing.pdf`): trace ट ठ ड ढ ण five times
each following the stroke arrows — saying each letter aloud as you write it — then the
syllable row टि टी टु टू ठा डे ढो णा. Final row: write घट, तट, गुण, गुड unaided. Check
every ट against every ठ: did the curve come home, or stay open (§15)?

**अभ्यासः 2 · वर्गपाठः (varga recital, record).** Record yourself reciting ट ठ ड ढ ण three
times with the full check kit — tissue, throat, nose — then all three learned rows in
sequence, then the twelve §14 words. Compare against the drill audio 🔊
(`planned:assets/audio/volume-1/v1c03l03-varga-drill.mp3`) and re-record only what
differs. Checklist: darker ring on every retroflex? Tissue jump on ठ alone? Murmur through
ढ? Final vowels full?

**अभ्यासः 3 · श्रवणभेदः (t/ṭ discrimination, 12 items).** A partner (or teacher) reads
twelve syllables, each either dental-side or retroflex-side, random order: from ता / टा,
ति / टि, तु / टु, ती / टी, ते / टे, तो / टो. For each item write what you heard (Devanagari
or IAST). Listen for the room-tone: the retroflex rings darker and hollower. 10/12 is a
pass; below that, redo §9 drill 4 and retest tomorrow — the contrast sharpens after sleep.

**अभ्यासः 4 · श्रुतलेखनम् (dictation).** Play the word-list audio 🔊
(`planned:assets/audio/volume-1/v1c03l03-word-list.mp3`) pausing after each word's first
reading, or have a partner read the twelve §14 words in random order. Write each in
Devanagari. Self-check against §14 with three questions per word: right retroflex letter
(ट/ठ? ड/ढ?)? Any Hindi ड़ that sneaked in? Final vowel written *and* said? 10/12 is a pass;
re-take tomorrow either way (§20).

**अभ्यासः 5 · स्पर्श-परीक्षा (the curl self-check, written).** Alternate English "ta" and
ट ten times, then English "da" and ड ten times. Now write three or four sentences in your
notebook answering: where exactly is your tongue tip for each of the two sounds? What do
you feel it pass on the way back? Which of the two sounds rings darker, and could you hear
it on your own recording from exercise 2? Naming the feeling in your own words is what
makes the gesture repeatable.

**अभ्यासः 6 · शब्दनिर्माणम् (word building, written).** Tiles: क ग घ ज त म ल · ट ठ ड ढ ण ·
ा ि ी ु ू ृ. Using only these (reuse allowed), build at least five real words from this
lesson or earlier ones and write them down. Bonus challenges: one word containing both a
त and a ट (§14 has it), one word with a breathy letter and a plain one, and the longest
word you can build. (A tile-word not on a course list needs a teacher's confirmation
before you trust it.)

sections.name: Quiz
sections.markdown:
प्रश्नाः — answers in the key at the end; no peeking mid-quiz.

1. For the ट-row, the tongue tip: (a) presses the upper teeth (b) rests at the alveolar
   ridge, as in English t (c) curls up and back behind the ridge (d) stays flat behind the
   lower teeth
2. Which letter is this row's tissue-thrower — the voiceless aspirate? (a) ट (b) ठ (c) ड
   (d) ढ
3. English t and d are ______, which makes them ______ of the Sanskrit retroflexes.
   (a) dental; identical twins (b) alveolar; next-door neighbors (c) retroflex; the same
   sounds (d) velar; distant relatives
4. A learner reads गुड aloud with a Hindi-style flap, "गुड़". What is the correct Sanskrit
   reading? (a) the flap is fine — same sound (b) guḍa — a full stop ड with complete
   contact, and the final अ pronounced (c) guḍ — full stop, no final vowel (d) gūḍa
5. Which word means "grass"? (a) गुण (b) तृण (c) कण (d) गण
6. On the page, ट and ठ differ because: (a) ठ closes into a full loop while ट stays an open
   bowl (b) ट carries a dot at its base (c) ठ has a vertical stem (d) they do not differ
7. Find the error: a learner reads गुण as "gun". Name both mistakes and give the correct
   reading.
8. Reading check — write the English meaning of each: (a) घट (b) तट (c) मूढ

<details><summary>उत्तराणि · Answer Key</summary>

1. (c) — curled up and back, past the ridge (§5, §11).
2. (b) ठ /ʈʰ/ — same curl, hard puff (§8, §15).
3. (b) alveolar; next-door neighbors — close enough to tempt, not close enough to be the
   sound (§5, §12 mistake 1).
4. (b) guḍa — Sanskrit has no ड़; full contact, full final vowel (§7, §12 mistake 2).
5. (b) तृण /t̪r̩ɳɐ/ (§14). (गुण "quality", कण "particle", गण "group".)
6. (a) open bowl vs closed loop (§15).
7. Two mistakes: the retroflex ण was flattened to a plain [n], and the final अ was dropped.
   Correct: guṇa /guɳɐ/ — tip curled through the nasal, final vowel full (§7, §12
   mistake 4, §14).
8. (a) घट = "pot"; (b) तट = "shore, bank"; (c) मूढ = "deluded, fool" (§14).
</details>

sections.name: Revision
sections.markdown:
पुनरावृत्तिः — one screen to remember.

> **The move:** curl the tip up and *past* the ridge, tap the dome — English t lives one
> door short. **The row (third run):** ट /ʈ/ plain — ठ /ʈʰ/ tissue-thrower — ड /ɖ/ buzzing
> — ढ /ɖʱ/ buzz + breath — ण /ɳ/ curled hum. **The letters:** ट open bowl, ठ closed loop;
> ड curls in, ढ loops on; ण alone wears a stem; ङ's dot ≠ ड's curl. **The traps:** don't
> settle at the ridge; Sanskrit गुड has no flap; ण is not [n]; the final अ stays. **The
> prize:** twelve words — घट तट कटु जटा कूट गुण गण कण तृण गुड गूढ मूढ — and a fully
> readable sentence: घटः अत्र अस्ति।

Spaced review (distributed practice beats cramming [REF:cepeda2006]):

- **In 1 day:** re-take the dictation (exercise 4) cold; write ट ठ ड ढ ण from memory and
  check ट/ठ and ड/ङ against the stroke card; one recital round with the tissue.
- **In 1 week:** record all three vargas back to back and compare with the drill audio;
  re-take the 12-item t/ṭ test (exercise 3); re-answer quiz Q4 and Q7 without looking.
- **From next lesson:** the dental row puts the tongue *on the teeth* — today's two-floor
  commute (ridge, curl) becomes a three-floor corridor, and the त/ट contrast becomes
  meaning-bearing. Keep the curl honest so tomorrow's contrast has room to live.

sections.name: Homework
sections.markdown:
गृहकार्यम् — about 30 minutes total.

1. **(10 min)** Finish exercises 1 and 4 if not completed in class: the tracing sheet and
   the first dictation pass.
2. **(5 min)** The recital with checks (§9 drill 2), three rounds — tissue on ठ, throat on
   ड, both on ढ, curled hum on ण.
3. **(10 min, real world)** Letter hunt: on any Hindi signboard, packet or newspaper, find
   and list eight words containing ट ठ ड ढ or ण (they are everywhere: टिकट, ठंडा, डाक,
   ढाबा…). Beside each, note whether it uses a plain ड/ढ or the flap letters ड़/ढ़ — you
   are training your eye to see the dot that Sanskrit never writes.
4. **(5 min, teach-back)** Teach someone the "one word, three tongues" drill (§9 drill 4)
   with English "tap". If you can guide their tongue from ridge to curl and they *hear*
   the darker ring, the gesture is yours.

Tomorrow, before anything else: the 1-day re-dictation (§20). The gap is the method.

sections.name: Teacher Notes
sections.markdown:
शिक्षक-टिप्पणी

**This is the feel lesson.** After the mirror lessons of Chapter 2, the key articulator is
now invisible — build the lesson on proprioception. Run the ridge walk (§9 drill 1) with
eyes closed, in silence, before any sound is made: tongue on teeth, slide to ridge, curl
past. Only then attach the voice. Students who "can't hear the difference" can almost
always *feel* it once the walk is slow enough.

**Timing plan (45 min):** §3 retrieval, written (5) → hook: English "tap" three ways, class
imitates (4) → ridge walk + curl-and-tap, then recital with checks (10) → the five cards
with the honest frequency notes (7) → board: grid row 3 + stroke work, ट/ठ and ड/ङ alarms
(8) → word list in pairs + dialogue (6) → exercises 3 and 5 setup (3) → homework briefing
incl. the 1-day re-dictation (2).

**Board work:** the 5×5 grid is the chapter's running board fixture — fill row 3 in front
of the class, saying each manner label as the letter lands. Draw ड and ङ side by side,
circle the dot and the curl, and leave them up all lesson.

**The two audiences split sharply today.** English speakers: their battle is mistake 1 —
the ridge feels like home. Give the "aim deeper than you need" license and let recordings
arbitrate. Hindi speakers: the sounds are native; their work is *suppression* — of the
automatic intervocalic flap (गुड ≠ गुड़) and of the colloquial ण→न merger — plus the
eternal final vowel. Be explicit that you are asking them to switch off a rule their mouth
applies without consulting them; naming it as a rule, not a fault, keeps the room on side.

**Use the Hindi speakers as models** for the curl itself (टमाटर runs on it), and pair them
with English speakers for exercise 3 — reading the stimulus list sharpens the reader as
much as the listener. Swap roles halfway.

**What students find hard:** ढ's murmur (re-run the घ tissue-plus-throat check from l01);
ण in isolation (no word begins with it, so drill it word-internally: गुण, तृण); and
believing that a sound that *sounds* right can still be wrong — the felt position, not the
ear, is the referee this week.

> घट, तट, गुण, गुड dotted once, then empty guided boxes for freehand. Footer: the chants
> "curve home = ठ, curve open = ट" and "dot is ङ — curl is ड". Generous spacing for child

sections.markdown:
Lesson video, ~6 min, presenter + motion graphics.

1. **Hook (0:00–0:40):** extreme close-up side-view animation of a tongue: it taps the
   ridge ("your English t"), then curls back and taps the dome — the screen darkens
   slightly and the audio rings deeper. Caption: "half a centimeter from English to
   Sanskrit". Title card: ट-वर्गः — The Retroflex Row.
2. **The ridge walk (0:40–1:50):** presenter guides the eyes-closed walk: teeth → ridge →
   curl, synced to the sagittal diagram (Asset 3) with the three stations lighting up.
   Recital with checks: tissue flutters on ठ, throat-buzz waveform on ड, both on ढ,
   nose-hum glow on ण.
3. **Five equal cards (1:50–3:00):** the five cards (Asset 1) slide in one by one, each
   with its check icon animating; honest frequency strips appear under ठ ड ढ ण with a
   presenter aside: "equal letters, unequal workloads — both true."
4. **Script alarms (3:00–4:00):** stroke-order animations for all five letters; then the
   two alarms as split-screens — ठ's loop snapping shut vs ट staying open; ङ's dot vs ड's
   curl pulsing in the highlight color.
5. **Words + the pot (4:00–5:10):** twelve word-cards fly in (Devanagari + IAST + gloss);
   गुड morphs briefly into Hindi गुड़ and back with a "no flap in Sanskrit" caption; the
   riverbank scene returns — Kamalā spots a clay pot on the तट, the five story lines play
   as captions, घटः highlighted letter-by-letter as fully readable.
6. **Recap + CTA (5:10–6:00):** the 5×5 grid fills its third row cell by cell; presenter
   reads घटः अत्र अस्ति one last time. End card: "12 words. Row three of five. Next: the
   row on your teeth." Dictation homework reminder overlay.

sections.name: Voice-over Script
sections.markdown:
Narration for the lesson video (§24). Sanskrit terms carry IPA cues in [brackets]; the
narrator reads them as IPA, not as English spelling.

- **00:00** Say "t". Your tongue just touched the ridge behind your teeth. Now curl the tip
  back — past the ridge — and tap the roof. ṭa [ʈɐ]. Hear that? Darker. Deeper. Half a
  centimeter, and you have left English.
- **00:25** These are the retroflexes — the sounds the world associates with India. The
  tradition calls the place mūrdhanya [muːrdʱɐnjɐ] — "of the crown of the head".
- **00:45** Close your eyes. Tongue on the teeth. Slide back — feel the bump? That ridge is
  English t's home. Keep going. Curl. Tap: ṭa [ʈɐ]. That path is the whole lesson.
- **01:15** Now the row you already know, third time through. ṭa [ʈɐ] — plain, no puff.
  ṭha [ʈʰɐ] — the tissue jumps. ḍa [ɖɐ] — the throat buzzes first. ḍha [ɖʱɐ] — buzz and
  breath together. ṇa [ɳɐ] — hum through the nose, tip still curled.
- **02:00** Five letters, honest facts: ṭa works everywhere. ṭha, ḍa, ḍha rarely *start* a
  word — inside words they are everywhere. And ṇa? No Sanskrit word begins with it. It
  lives in the middle — guṇa [guɳɐ], tṛṇa [t̪r̩ɳɐ].
- **02:40** Writing time. ṭa is an open bowl. ṭha closes the loop — that is the whole
  difference. ḍa curls in at the base; ḍha loops once more — extra breath, extra ink. And
  ṇa is the only one with a stem.
- **03:20** Watch out: the velar nasal ends in a dot. ḍa ends in a curl. Dot — curl. Write
  them side by side once, and you will never mix them.
- **03:45** Twelve words. ghaṭa [gʱɐʈɐ] — a pot. taṭa [t̪ɐʈɐ] — a riverbank. kaṭu [kɐʈu] —
  bitter. jaṭā [d͡ʑɐʈɑː] — matted hair. kūṭa [kuːʈɐ] — a peak, or a trick. guṇa [guɳɐ] —
  a quality — or a strand of rope. gaṇa [gɐɳɐ], kaṇa [kɐɳɐ], tṛṇa [t̪r̩ɳɐ] — group, grain,
  grass.
- **04:20** And three for your tongue's discipline: guḍa [guɖɐ] — jaggery. Hindi speakers:
  no flap here — the tongue parks, full stop. gūḍha [guːɖʱɐ] — hidden. mūḍha [muːɖʱɐ] —
  the fool it stays hidden from. Breath all the way through the ḍha [ɖʱɐ].
- **04:50** The pot, by the way, is famous. When Sanskrit philosophers need "some object",
  they reach for a clay pot: ghaṭaḥ asti [gʱɐʈɐhɐ ɐst̪i] — "the pot exists". You can now
  read the philosophers' favorite prop.
- **05:15** Down at the riverbank, Kamalā has found one: mama ghaṭaḥ! mama taṭaḥ! My pot,
  my riverbank — and this time she can read every letter, tail included.
- **05:40** Twelve words. Three rows of the grid. Next lesson, the tongue lands on the
  teeth — and t against ṭ starts changing meanings. Keep the curl honest until then.
  ghaṭa [gʱɐʈɐ]. Take the pot with you.

sections.name: Reel Script
sections.markdown:
40–50 seconds, vertical, captions burned in.

- **Hook (0:00–0:07):** side-view tongue animation, snap zoom. Presenter: "Your English T
  is half a centimeter away from Sanskrit. Watch."
- **Demo (0:07–0:30):** presenter, slow-motion mouth shots: "Tongue on the ridge — ta.
  Now curl it back — ṭa [ʈɐ]. Hear how it got darker? That's a retroflex." Rapid recital
  with icons: ट ठ ड ढ ण — tissue jumps on ठ. "And Hindi speakers — you own these. One
  catch: Sanskrit गुड has no flap. Full stop, full vowel: guḍa [guɖɐ]."
- **Payoff (0:30–0:42):** word-wall: घट तट गुण गुड गूढ मूढ; a clay pot icon lands on घट.
  "Twelve new words — including the pot Indian philosophers argue about: ghaṭa [gʱɐʈɐ]."
- **CTA (0:42–0:50):** "This is Sanskritam. Next: the row that lives on your teeth — and
  the day t versus ṭ starts changing meanings. Follow and feel the difference." (End card:
  ट-वर्गः — The Retroflex Row.)

quiz.questions_markdown:
प्रश्नाः — answers in the key at the end; no peeking mid-quiz.

1. For the ट-row, the tongue tip: (a) presses the upper teeth (b) rests at the alveolar
   ridge, as in English t (c) curls up and back behind the ridge (d) stays flat behind the
   lower teeth
2. Which letter is this row's tissue-thrower — the voiceless aspirate? (a) ट (b) ठ (c) ड
   (d) ढ
3. English t and d are ______, which makes them ______ of the Sanskrit retroflexes.
   (a) dental; identical twins (b) alveolar; next-door neighbors (c) retroflex; the same
   sounds (d) velar; distant relatives
4. A learner reads गुड aloud with a Hindi-style flap, "गुड़". What is the correct Sanskrit
   reading? (a) the flap is fine — same sound (b) guḍa — a full stop ड with complete
   contact, and the final अ pronounced (c) guḍ — full stop, no final vowel (d) gūḍa
5. Which word means "grass"? (a) गुण (b) तृण (c) कण (d) गण
6. On the page, ट and ठ differ because: (a) ठ closes into a full loop while ट stays an open
   bowl (b) ट carries a dot at its base (c) ठ has a vertical stem (d) they do not differ
7. Find the error: a learner reads गुण as "gun". Name both mistakes and give the correct
   reading.
8. Reading check — write the English meaning of each: (a) घट (b) तट (c) मूढ
quiz.answer_key_markdown:
1. (c) — curled up and back, past the ridge (§5, §11).
2. (b) ठ /ʈʰ/ — same curl, hard puff (§8, §15).
3. (b) alveolar; next-door neighbors — close enough to tempt, not close enough to be the
   sound (§5, §12 mistake 1).
4. (b) guḍa — Sanskrit has no ड़; full contact, full final vowel (§7, §12 mistake 2).
5. (b) तृण /t̪r̩ɳɐ/ (§14). (गुण "quality", कण "particle", गण "group".)
6. (a) open bowl vs closed loop (§15).
7. Two mistakes: the retroflex ण was flattened to a plain [n], and the final अ was dropped.
   Correct: guṇa /guɳɐ/ — tip curled through the nasal, final vowel full (§7, §12
   mistake 4, §14).
8. (a) घट = "pot"; (b) तट = "shore, bank"; (c) मूढ = "deluded, fool" (§14).

registers.text: The traditional phonetics texts — the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā and the Prātiśākhyas — file ट ठ ड ढ ण as मूर्धन्य (mūrdhanya), from मूर्धन् (mūrdhan) "head, crown": sounds made with the tongue reaching up toward the dome that crowns the mouth's interior. The name is an articulation diagram compressed into one word.

Retroflexion is one of South Asia's great shared features: Sanskrit and its Indo-Aryan descendants have it, and the neighboring Dravidian family (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) uses it even more richly — a convergence built over millennia of contact. But the sound type holds no passport: Swedish and Norwegian produce retroflex [ʈ ɖ ɳ] in their *rt, rd, rn* words, and several Australian languages maintain full retroflex series of their own. [REF:masica1991]

ट ठ ड ढ ण are retroflex stops — /ʈ ʈʰ ɖ ɖʱ ɳ/: the tongue **tip** curls up and back to strike the roof of the mouth *behind* the alveolar ridge. The curled posture opens a small hollow beneath the tongue, which is why retroflexes ring darker and more cavernous than their front-of-the-mouth cousins. [REF:ladefoged2015]

English t and d are alveolar — made *at* the ridge. On the mouth's map that puts them closer to retroflex ट/ड than to dental त/द: one small retraction away from the first, a full tongue-posture change away from the second. English ears therefore accept an alveolar t as "close enough" for either row — which is exactly why the dental row (next lesson) will need an explicit teeth-contact contrast. [REF:ladefoged2015]
The manner frame is unchanged: voiceless, voiceless aspirated, voiced, voiced breathy, nasal. Only the *place* is new — master one tongue-curl and all five letters follow. [REF:whitney1889 §§39–50]

Frequency, honestly: ट is common in all positions; ठ ड ढ begin few native Sanskrit words but occur freely word-internally; ण essentially never opens a word and is everywhere inside them. Equal cards, unequal workloads — both facts on the same card. [REF:apte1890]

In the Nyāya school of Indian logic, the pot is the stock example-object: घटः अस्ति (ghaṭaḥ asti) "the pot exists" is the demonstration sentence a beginning logic student meets on page one, the way English philosophy reaches for Socrates. Where an argument needs "some thing", the tradition hands it a pot.

गुण's dictionary entry fans out from the concrete to the abstract: a strand or cord — of a rope, a bowstring — then a quality, an attribute, a virtue. One concrete image carrying a family of abstract senses is a pattern Sanskrit vocabulary loves; you will watch this particular word work hard across the whole tradition. [REF:apte1890 s.v. गुण]

Four of today's letters — ट ठ ड ढ — carry no right-hand vertical stem; ण is the row's only stem-bearer. Mātrās adapt without new rules: ि and ी stand in their usual places (टि, टी), and the below-signs hang from the base of the curve — टु, टू, as they hang from ट's bowl. Position is graphics; order is speech — unchanged. [REF:masica1991 ch.6]

One more thing today's letters can spell: कठ (kaṭha) — the name of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, the celebrated dialogue in which young Naciketas questions Death itself. Its story waits for Volume 5; as of today, you can read its name.
